  holds considerable promise for the management of respiratory conditions such as

  the development of user-friendly, portable monitoring devices capable of guiding 
  respiratory self-management. Furthermore, this study provides valuable insights 
  into the design of such devices, highlighting the importance of device-based 
  solutions that can be used in the early stages of respiratory symptoms.

This behavior contrasts with that of radio jets in active galactic nuclei, which typically exhibit minimal variations. A possible interpretation of this phenomenon draws on a theory originally proposed for blazars, suggesting that the optical and UV spectra in these galaxies are produced by electrons interacting with photons within their environment. To accurately determine these distributions, we employed a data-driven approach based on correcting pp collision data by incorporating information from heavy-ion collisions.  Specifically, we utilized corrected data to constrain fits of strange quark distribution functions in protons using quantum chromodynamics, and found that these fits were largely unaffected by variations in input parameters. To address these challenges, we developed novel methods to calculate measures of bias in NLP, drawing on graphical models and information theory. To train models on these datasets, we utilized a fairness-aware risk estimator, incorporating both the prejudice inherent in the model's loss function and the prejudice embedded in the underlying data distribution.  To assess the presence of embedded bias in our models, we employed a fairness-aware inverse propensity score estimator.  To validate the modularity of our design, we conducted additional experiments using pre-trained models and a simplified version of our fairness-aware approach.  The results of our experiments showed that traditional methods fail to account for the influence of visual elements on context and, consequently, result in models that exhibit significant bias in relation to certain aspects of context, notably age and ethnicity.  Furthermore, we discovered that models trained on modality-agnostic text context often manifest embedded bias, even in the absence of explicit bias in the underlying data distribution. This shift is driven by a growing interest in earlier, more specific clinical trials that can be guided by multiple biomarkers, potentially opening up new avenues for precision medicine. However, this shift also introduces significant design difficulties, particularly when trying to match both efficiency and effectiveness in biomarker trials. In this paper, we explore the ideal design of a single-biomarker trial using a threshold-based binary endpoint, and present an optimal stopping strategy that achieves optimal performance in two key areas: statistical power and required sample size. We show that this optimal strategy has performance comparable to traditional methods in some cases, and significantly better than these methods in others. Furthermore, we establish that the optimal sample size required under this strategy decreases at a minimum rate of $1/\sqrt{k}$, where $k$ is a parameter that depends on the trial's desired level of precision and sensitivity to the biomarker. We also introduce an approximate stopping rule that scales linearly with the estimated mean of the biomarker, and demonstrate its advantages in standard scenarios. In addition, we provide recommendations for choosing $k$ in practice, and discuss potential extensions to multi-biomarker trials. Finally, we conclude by emphasizing the potential benefits and challenges of threshold-based clinical trials, and highlight the need for further statistical research in this area. We accompany this paper with a supplementary code that facilitates easy implementation of the proposed optimal and approximate stopping rules in trials involving continuous biomarkers. We believe that this paper and its accompanying code offer valuable tools that can be used by researchers and clinicians working together to design more efficient clinical trials for precision medicine. of inverse problems involving the Boltzmann transport equation, which models the interaction between electrons and phonons within graphene. This equation features a high-frequency component that hinders the resolution of the initial distribution function, particularly in early time frames. The proposed algorithm addresses this issue by utilizing a hybrid differential scheme that combines molecular dynamics and the solution of the Boltzmann transport equation. This approach yields a solution for the initial conditions, including the high-energy electron distribution, which would otherwise be inaccessible due to the short time frame of such events. Ultimately, the proposed method facilitates a deeper understanding of the inverse photoemission process in graphene and allows for the prediction of the initial electron distribution following the injection of photons into the material. 

The code for the proposed algorithm is available at: https://github.com/numericalmaterial/BTEInverse.

This approach is based on two assumptions: either the two highest-energy particles escape undetected, or the two protons collide head-on. By comparing the observed data to simulated events under these two scenarios, a comprehensive picture of all possible hadronic outcomes can be obtained.   To investigate the system's performance on curved tracks, the model considers both circular arcs and Helix-shaped tracks. Our study focuses on a specific train, the CR400, but the proposed track-following control method can be applied to other trains with similar curved track conditions. 

  In our simulation, we find that the 2-CLB model accurately replicates the real train's yawing phenomenon on curved tracks. However, this phenomenon causes the bogie to deviate from the desired circular path, posing a challenge for track-following control systems. 

  To address this issue, we developed a 2-DOF (2-dimensional, degree-of-freedom) model-based controller that takes into account the bogie's complex yawing dynamics. 

  Our simulation results show that this controller effectively reduces the yawing amplitude and ensures the system stays within a $2\sigma$ tolerance limit for a curved track with a small radius. 

  Furthermore, our study highlights the importance of accurately modeling the bogie's yawing dynamics when designing track-following control systems for curved tracks. 

  To validate our theoretical findings, we conducted physical experiments on a curved track with a medium radius using a scaled-down 2-CLB model, and the results matched our simulation predictions. 

  Our proposed track-following control system has been implemented in the CR400 train, and the system's performance can be continuously refined as more data becomes available. 

  In conclusion, our study provides an efficient and reliable solution for tracking control systems on curved tracks, offering a reference for other train models with similar dynamics.

  In particular, we believe that our 2-DOF controller can be adapted for use in other applications involving cellular lattice bogies, such as braking systems, by considering the bogie's longitudinal dynamics.

Dubbed "surface evolution", this technique employs a system of partial differential equations to smoothly alter an object's surface based on local energy minimization principles.  Despite its potential, applying surface evolution to real-world problems is hindered by the need for manual writing of algorithms in MATLAB, as well as the lack of publicly available code and evolving curves in the Lagrangian framework.  To address these limitations, we developed a method using level set methods to solve surface evolution equations, making it suitable for production-scale implementation and publicly available. In order to further explore the applicability of surface evolution to computer vision tasks, we also experimented with using it as a feature extractor in a shape recognition system.  The results showed that although surface evolution has a high initial learning curve, with the right approach, it can effectively learn and generalize to various tasks.  In particular, we found that adding surface evolution to a convolutional neural network led to enhanced performance when processing complex shapes.  In conclusion, we propose integrating surface evolution with deep networks as a way to enhance their performance, particularly when processing shapes that require minimal energy transformation.   This research focuses on a class of models where dynamics is governed

  Specifically, we investigated the influence of both periodic and

  In the classical domain, we observed the aperiodic behavior through
  power spectrum analysis and the application of the Fruhlingsheim-Melhado

  We found that the effects of aperiodic driving result in reduced
  quantum coherence, outpacing the impact of periodic driving.
  Consequently, our findings imply that the quantum system tends to
  "remember" the aperiodic component of the classical driver's a
  ("sensitive to initial conditions") behavior more than the
  ("rotationally symmetric") aspect. 
  This contrast to classical dynamics' Halpern-Hammish effect highlights
  the distinct response to a driver of two different quantum systems. 
  In the aperiodically driven case, we also observed that the
  coherence decay accelerates with increased aperiodic driving,
  offering a concrete example of quantum chaos manifested as
  increased error in quantum operations, specifically state preparation
  and quantum computations based on those states. 
  Our research suggests that a quantum system driven by an aperiodic
  Hamiltonian may fail to meet quantum reliability standards,
  providing motivation for carefully selecting the set of classical
  drivers in experimental setups. 
  This research has implications for quantum simulations of black holes,
  quantum computers based on continuous-time driving, and
  quantum gravity experiments via interferometry. 
  In conclusion, we propose a strategy for detecting chaos in
  quantum systems, relying on the aperiodic component of the
  power spectrum of phase-space coherence. 
  This analysis can be applied to a wide range of models, offering
  a concrete example of quantum error caused by a classical driver's
  aperiodic behavior that could be challenging to differentiate from
  other sources of error, such as shot noise. 
  We emphasize the significance of carefully selecting the set of
  classical drivers in experimental setups to minimize quantum error. 
  This may entail driving frequencies that allow for easy state
  preparation and computation, potentially sacrificing a tiny

orthogonal polynomial bases for all orders using numerical methods is addressed. We establish an integral equation expression for the basis coefficients, presenting a computational framework that utilizes Gauss-Kronquist quadrature. This approach enables the creation of discrete orthogonal polynomial bases at any degree, offering a solution to the common challenge of maintaining orthogonality properties when basis transformations are applied. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our construction results in bases with decreasing norm, meeting the standards set by Zhidkov's criteria. Consequently, our method produces, for the first time, orthogonal polynomial bases with all possible degrees via numerical means, eliminating the need for recursive procedures. This achievement is particularly significant for the use of orthogonal polynomials in Gaussian quadrature, providing an alternative to time-consuming recursive methods to find the coefficients of the basis transformation, and offering a scalable solution for degree increases. Moreover, we utilized this framework to assemble a set of discrete orthogonal polynomial bases of extreme degrees (extremal points) necessary for Gauss quadrature, resulting in an improvement in the computed integral estimates compared to standard approaches. Our findings indicate that extremal point bases with a limited degree can yield more accurate results than commonly employed degree-d bases, suggesting a promising strategy for determining the optimal basis degree in practice. This research was conducted using MATLAB R2020a, running on a Windows 10 Pro platform, and the developed code is available online for the convenience of potential users. To illustrate the applicability of this method, we utilized it to refine the estimates of integral domains previously proposed by Temme, covering a wider range of domains, including the Schönhage-Elkies domain, and our code is capable of handling degrees up to 5000 or more, depending on the chosen method parameters. Additionally, we emphasize the flexibility of this approach, highlighting that any increase in the desired degree simply requires the computation of a corresponding set of nodes and coefficients via the described method. Consequently, our research involves further refining the parameters of this method for specific applications, as well as exploring alternative numerical approaches to maintain scalability with higher degrees. Along the way, we encountered the challenge of maintaining the integrity of the orthogonal property when utilizing variable-precision arithmetic, and we outline a proposal for a more robust implementation that utilizes the property of discrete orthogonal polynomials with reduced norm. This proposal involves developing a module that utilizes the described framework, incorporating a variable-precision arithmetic strategy based on Montgomery's multiplication method, and our goal is to refine this module further, exploring better arithmetic strategies and more efficient data structures to enhance the performance of the algorithm

  be challenging to navigate. Moreover, we discovered that some actions can 
  modify project metadata, potentially leading to unexpected consequences 
  during security analyses. Additionally, many actions utilize unverified 
  community-created repositories. To mitigate these risks, we propose several 
  guidelines for action developers, including providing clear documentation, 
  utilizing verified repositories, and employing secure practices when using

  surrounding mediums, paving the way for a deeper comprehension of 
  non-linear particle acceleration processes in the universe.

set of Möbius transformations that map the real line to itself, and let $\bar{G}$ be the group consisting of these transformations, where the group operation is composition.  Define the projection map $\pi$ from $\bar{G}$ to the set of bijective mappings of the real line as ignoring the pre and image values of the transformations.  This paper explores the structure of the quotient group $\bar{G}/\pi$ and identifies $\pi$-invariant properties. In a distributed blockchain setting, this is typically achieved through consensus protocols that force all nodes to agree on the blockchain's state, while also preventing a single malicious node from controlling the network.  In this work, we investigate the fault tolerance of a specific blockchain architecture that utilizes a two-party system, where a group of users compete to include new blocks in the blockchain, and a group of validators compete to verify these blocks. 

  We establish conditions under which this architecture enables the blockchain to withstand a single malicious user and provide a strategy for making it fault-tolerant in the presence of $f$ malicious users, where the degree of fault tolerance grows proportionally with the network's size.  In analyzing this architecture, we find that the order of blocks influences the effectiveness of its consensus protocol, leading to it being classified as a type of graph-based blockchain protocol. 

  We also demonstrate that all graph-based blockchain protocols are vulnerable to an attack that blocks the progress of the blockchain, before establishing conditions under which the two-party system can withstand this type of attack if the order of blocks is chosen randomly. 

  In exploring real-world applications, we show that the two-party system matches the efficiency of leading blockchain protocols, such as DeFi platforms, and is scalable enough to support these platforms. 

  In concluding, we highlight the implications of our work for the design of graph-based blockchain protocols.

is characterized by quantum fluctuations that  
  preclude the formation of magnetic long-range order, and it is often sought  
  to identify materials exhibiting this state. This study focuses on Ba$_3$Cr$_{1-x}$Ga$_x$Ti$_{1+x}$O$_{12}$, a magnetically dilute and three-dimensional material that is expected to harbor a QSL state. By examining magnetic susceptibility, inelastic scattering from this material, researchers were able to confirm the absence of a QSL state and instead found a clear indication of a one-dimensional, anisotropic Heisenberg chain with a small finite-size correction. Using numerical methods, scientists simulated the magnetic excitation spectrum of this chain and found that although it shows a general quasiparticle peak, it also exhibits significant scattering just above the lower bound of a continuum, a feature that is a result of a combination of a very small next nearest neighbor interaction and a moderate next to next nearest neighbor interaction. To further understand this spectrum, researchers compared it with a N\'{e}el state of the same Heisenberg chain and found that although both spectra exhibit a quasiparticle peak, the continuum in the N\'{e}el state is more pronounced and occurs at a higher energy, a feature that can be attributed to the presence of three-magnon bound state in the N\'{e}el state. A fair agreement between the simulated and experimental spectra can be achieved by introducing a small broadening and a variation in the exchange interactions along the chain. A future study of this material with a higher concentration of chromium could potentially exhibit a QSL state, a result that would be a rare occurrence in a three-dimensional, magnetically dilute arrangement. To that end, researchers recommend further study of this material with a focus on modifying the chromium content while also exploring other possible magnetic ground states of this material. Based on the findings from this study, researchers propose the Ba$_3$Cr$_{1-x}$Ga$_x$Ti$_{1+x}$O$_{12}$ chain as a potential candidate for a QSL state that can be manipulated and studied through chemical modification. A possible future direction of study could also involve a comparison with Ba$_3$TiCr$_{1+x}$O$_{12}$, a material that exhibits a similar structure but with a different arrangement of magnetic ions.

A comprehensive model incorporating the hard X-ray AGN component, the contribution from the host galaxy, and the scatter as a function of luminosity was employed.  The analysis reveals that the excess emission in the  10^44-10^46 erg/s/s extragalactic space velocity frame can be described as a non-extensive Boltzmann distribution with a k-factor of around 10 and a q-factor of about 1.1-1.2 for the specified energy range and assuming a photon index of around 2.5-3.5 for the AGN component.  The study also estimates the excess radiation power as a function of frame energy and finds that the characteristic energy can rise with increasing frame energy, potentially linked to the interaction between the AGN jet and the surrounding medium.  The research suggests that the excess emission in the hard X-ray range is a natural extension of the observed optical/UV continuum, and the combination of all observed components results in an estimated total bolometric luminosity of around 10^46-10^47 erg/s/s for the studied quasars. ers, an enhanced version of the adiabatic perturbation theory specifically tailored to address the universe's evolution when it was nearly frictionless. This theory enables us to treat perturbations as independent dynamical systems while accounting for the impact of dark matter and dark energy dynamics. We demonstrate that adiabatic perturbation theory can be expanded beyond its traditional application to the universe's early stages. Consequently, we can accurately model the development of perturbations during a period when the Hubble parameter experienced rapid growth, a phase that is crucial for understanding the formation of super-Hubble scales. We further show that a quarter of the scale factor is an optimal lower bound for applying this expanded theory, as it ensures that adiabatic perturbation theory is no longer significantly inaccurate by this point. Within the expanded framework, we calculate the modes' evolution during a phase of rapid Hubble expansion and find that they follow a universal power-law pattern, with growth that is directly influenced by the scale of the mode. We believe that the Greenformers approach offers a valuable, computationally efficient alternative to numerical implementations of perturbation theory for modes with Hubble-sized scales, with applications in both the early universe and its late stages. We also propose that future work could explore the expansion of perturbation theory in other contexts. In the United States alone, between 2004 and 2014, there were over a billion dollars in economic losses due to landslides, soil erosion and debris flow, with the deadliest event being the 2014 Oso mudslide in Washington that killed 43 people.  Sediment-displacing floods, wildfires, storms and freezing temperatures can all trigger landslides.  Research on landslides focuses on the movement of soil and rock, but not typically the initial displacement that sets them in motion.  This article discusses a specific type of landslide called debris flow that occurs when rain causes soil to become saturated and mix with forest debris, leading to trees being uprooted and landslides that block rivers and cause devastating floods.  An in-depth examination is given of the 2018 Montecristi landslide in the Dominican Republic that killed 39 people, before presenting a debris flow model that includes the movement of interacting fluid and particle components.  This model was tested using data from a 2019 experiment in an outdoor flume in Italy, and also the data from the Montecristi landslide, revealing that the model captures the blocking of rivers by landslides and the resulting floods that follow.  This research provides the basis for a future model that can predict the initiation of debris flows, and is currently limited by a lack of understanding of the initial saturation of soil.  This article also includes supplementary material such as raw data from the Montecristi landslide, images and videos.  This research was supported by grants from NASA and NSF, and in collaboration with researchers from the Dominican Republic, Italy, and the US.  This article is accompanied by a video explaining the Montecristi landslide in the words of the people who lived through it, and a video showing the flume experiment in Italy.  This research aims to contribute to the development of early warning systems for landslides and floods, and is part of a broader initiative to study and model the movement of interacting fluid and particle components in natural disasters.  This article is also accompanied by a graphical abstract, and a figure showing the flume experiment in Italy.  This research has important implications for predicting and preventing landslides and floods, and is currently being expanded to model the movement of landslides that block rivers and cause devastating floods, and the movement of landslides in forests that cause tree uprooting and landslides. from Diverse Experiences (TELDE) framework for training autonomous ground vehicles in path-following tasks via reinforcement learning. The algorithm addresses several challenges associated with reinforcement learning, including the need for vast amounts of data, slow training processors, and unreliable sensors in vehicles. 

  TELDE consists of two main components: a tracking-error agent that uses a simple reinforcement learning model to train a vehicle to follow a target path in an easy environment, and an expert agent trained in a more complex environment using supervised learning, with the policy determined by the tracking-error agent. 

  The algorithm incorporates an innovative diversity-enhancing mechanism to promote exploration and prevent overfitting, with performance demonstrated on a publicly available dataset for both urban and highway driving scenarios. 

  Evaluations show that TELDE achieves better results compared to a baseline model trained using the collected data without diversity learning, with the algorithm's code available at https://github.com/DAI-LAB/TELDE. 

  Future work involves applying the TELDE framework to other challenging autonomous driving tasks. 

  The code for the TELDE framework is available at https://github.com/DAI-LAB/TELDE. 

  For the detailed technical report, please see https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.07751. 

  The code and technical report can be utilized as a starting point for developing diverse and efficient learning strategies for other autonomous driving tasks. 

  The dataset used in this paper is publicly available at https://www.daibench.org/. 

  The Daibench platform enables the creation, editing, and management of diverse, high-quality driving datasets with diverse driving experiences for the community, with the goal of advancing autonomous driving research through collaborative, dataset-driven efforts. 

  The code, technical report, and Daibench platform are all open-source. 

  The Daibench platform is available at https://www.daibench.org/. 

  The code for the TELDE framework and Daibench platform can be installed using pip with the command `pip install telde daibench`. 

  The TELDE framework and Daibench platform are designed to be highly customizable and scalable, with the code and technical report intended as a starting point and resources for further research and development. 

  The algorithm, framework, and platform are developed by a team led by Dr. Stefan Lee at the Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence. 

  The research and development are supported by the National Science Foundation and Amazon Robotics.

\mathcal{PT}$) symmetry, plays a crucial role 
  in controlling and manipulating light-matter interactions within photonic systems. 
  Originally proposed by Berry in 1989, $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric optics was not 
  explored until 2011, when a photonic crystal slab exhibiting $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric 
  properties was successfully created. This review delves into the fundamental principles 
  of $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric optics and its various implementations, including 
  $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric metasurfaces, lattices with $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric 
  non-Hermitian Hamiltonians, and $\mathcal{K}$-$\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric systems. 
  It also examines the $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric phase transition and its associated 
  $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric mode coupling, as well as its applications in sensing 
  and imaging. Furthermore, this review discusses the integration of $\mathcal{PT}$ 
  symmetry with artificial magnetism, electromagnetism, and electromechanics. 
  Finally, it presents an in-depth examination of $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric optics 
  through the lens of wave function center-of-mass transformations, allometric 
  growth in non-Hermitian systems, and the $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric phase 
  transition's statistical physics. This review aims to provide a comprehensive 
  overview of the latest developments in $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric optics, 
  as well as its potential applications and integrated devices. 
  Specifically, it highlights the emergence of $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric 
  dynamics in coupled cavities, the integration of $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric 
  systems with artificial magnetism and electromagnetism, and the potential 
  benefits of utilizing $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric optics in high-speed 
  sensing and imaging. This review concludes by outlining the key challenges 
  and potential avenues for future research in the field of $\mathcal{PT}$ 
  optics. This review originated from an invited talk at the 2021 International 
  Conference on Quantum Dots and Photon Counting, and it is intended to serve 
  as a comprehensive overview of the subject for graduate students and 
  young researchers in related fields.

in stellar cores, magnetohydrodynamic simulations must efficiently handle the vast difference between the macroscopic and microscopic scales characteristic of these systems. To achieve this, a balanced approach is taken in the MAGIX code, employing a combination of large-eddy simulation and the dissipation of remaining fluctuations by turbulent mixing-length theory. This method is used to model the influence of turbulent velocities on the movement and mixing of magnetic field lines. A key aspect of the MAGIX approach is the use of an unresolved turbulence closure model, which is a new feature compared to previous versions of the code. This model specifically addresses the variation of the mixing-length parameter with the angle between the magnetic field and the gradient of the plasma density. Such a model can be applied to the study of solar magnetic flux tubes and instabilities within these tubes, as well as to rotating stars and rotating magnetic flux tubes. An important area for future development of the MAGIX code is improving its magnetic field resolution. This can be achieved by either utilizing a more advanced numerical method or incorporating an interpolation technique that preserves magnetic monopoles. Such advancements are crucial for accurately modeling important processes, such as magnetic breakdown and Ohm's law, through direct numerical means rather than through semi-empirical parameterizations. This will likely involve a significant increase in the computational resources required for the simulations. Alternatively, better understanding of how magnetohydrodynamic turbulence influences turbulent transport, particularly in stellar cores, is also necessary for further improvements to the MAGIX code. This can be achieved by either incorporating an empirical closure model or utilizing a simulation that can resolve the spatial structure of the turbulence. Such a resolution would allow for a more realistic modeling of the mixing-length parameter and its variation with the angle, which is critical for accurately interpreting data from the MAGIX code, particularly in regards to solar magnetic flux tubes and rotating magnetic flux tubes. This includes investigating how the distribution of the $\alpha$-parameter changes with the angle in a variety of settings, as well as exploring the implications of different closure models on this distribution. This research is presented in a companion paper. This involves analyzing the magnetohydrodynamic simulations that were used to inform the MAGIX code, as well as the code's results and how they compare to observations and other models. This includes examining the spatial and temporal distribution of the $\alpha$-parameter, as well as its variation with the angle and the strength of the magnetic field. This research provides a critical understanding of the assumptions and limitations of the MAGIX code, which is necessary for its further development and improvements

If these systems are accessible through online platforms, training accurate facial recognition models through transfer learning might be feasible, thus nullifying their utility.  Conversely, making private systems too difficult to breach could necessitate costly customized security solutions.  This research investigates how accessible current public facial recognition systems are through model stealing attacks.  A widely used pre-trained facial recognition model was fine-tuned using transfer learning on 10 publicly available datasets featuring European and Asian faces, and the results showed that even with heavily restricted fine-tuning, the derived model was highly effective at recognizing faces, particularly those found in certain datasets used for European facial feature detection.  Ultimately, our findings indicate that many free public facial recognition systems might not be as secure as anticipated, and potential users should carefully review system development details before utilizing them.  This research also contributes a set of reproducible models and data, and our top dataset-based feature extraction model is available for download at our website.  In addition, we detail a novel multi-step pipeline featuring a publicly accessible facial recognition system, and our study's design, methods, and findings are all grounded in existing literature citations.  In conclusion, researchers, system developers, and potential users of public facial recognition systems at large need to be aware of and address the existing model stealing attack vulnerability.  Finally, our research highlights the pressing need for novel security solutions to safeguard against these attacks.  In particular, we propose that developers should implement systematic security evaluations to prevent model stealing attacks by assessing the accuracy of derived models produced by users, and our approach to doing so is detailed in the recommended future work section of this paper. electrical fluctuations at the top of a tethered spacecraft to determine its 
floating potential and subsequently, the electron flux near the spacecraft 
surface. This method provides a non-intrusive approach to studying electron 
flux in various environments. However, the underlying theory assumes that the 
spacecraft's sheath field causes all electron impacts to result in repulsive 
scatters, leading to a specific relationship between current fluctuations and 
time. Recent experiments on the ISS have deviated from this expectation, 
exhibiting different Reimann noise spectra than predicted. To address this 
discrepancy, we employed a more advanced model of current fluctuations, based 
on the Langevin method, which takes into account the impact of electron 
scatters and the dynamics of the spacecraft's electric field. Using data from the 
FPF experiment on the ISS, our results confirm that the models accurately 
match observed Reimann noise spectra. Furthermore, we identified two distinct 
components of noise in the data: a larger component attributed to changes 
in electron flux, and a smaller component thought to be linked to variations 
in electron temperature. Moreover, our analysis enables retrieval of both 
electron flux and electron temperature values from the measured data, 
enabling a more comprehensive understanding of the environment near the 
spacecraft surface. To further explore this knowledge, we propose an enhanced 
FPF analysis that incorporates both components of noise, utilizing a 
combination of theoretical modeling and experimental data from the ISS, 
specifically from the Earth-facing side. To facilitate replication of the 
results presented, we have made our data processing code available for 
academic use. Moreover, our findings imply that future FPF-type experiments 
should utilize shorter tethers to minimize sheath field effects and 
potentially detect additional information, such as electron energy spectra. 
Additionally, we propose possible applications of this enhanced analysis in 
contexts like planetary exploration, emphasizing the value of integrating 
electrical measurements with physical properties of the surrounding plasma. 
Finally, we outline potential design improvements for future experiments, 
including adjustable tethers and enhanced current sensors, as well as a 
suggested format for incorporating electron flux estimates into existing data 
models used for this purpose.

  between synthetic and actual wavefields. Despite its potential, FWI often
  gets stuck at local minima due to its non-linear and computationally
  intensive nature. To address this challenge, we present a data misfit
  function that accounts for the differences in wavefields at multiple time
  steps, combining the benefits of both waveform and phase difference
  mismatches. This new formulation enables the use of both actual and
  synthetic wavefields in our calculations, eliminating the need to
  re-solve the inverse problem for each iteration of time steps. We also
  introduce a hybrid optimization algorithm that employs both gradient-based
  and stochastic methods to address the non-linear and complex nature of
  FWI. To assess and evaluate the performance of this new approach, we
  apply it to two numerical examples featuring real-earth models and
  challenging geological structures. The results show that our FWI method
  delivers significant improvements in model updates and accelerates the
  convergence to physically meaningful structures, reducing the number of
  iterations required to obtain a globally minimum solution.  Specially,
  synthetic data analysis indicates that our method can recover the
  location, orientation, and properties of complex geological features
  such as faults, cavities, and fluid-saturated regions with high
  accuracy. To further explore the practical feasibility of this new method

  integrating it with other seismic imaging techniques.  Ultimately, our

To evaluate the effectiveness of such a dataset, we utilize standard adversarial learning metrics and assess how it affects the network's resilience in various scenarios, including data augmentation that either positively or negatively impacts the network, and the potential harm caused by using incorrect training data. technology allows electric vehicles to supply energy
  back to the power grid when they are parked. This innovation has the
  potential to provide additional income for vehicle owners and support the
  stability of the electrical system by consuming excess energy during periods
  of high demand. Furthermore, the vast number of V2G devices connected to
  the grid may offer system resilience by adjusting energy consumption as other
  power sources become unavailable. This study develops a double-layered V2G
  system model that takes into consideration both individual profit and
  global energy stability. It then employs a decentralized intelligent agent
  framework to manage V2G devices. The proposed approach includes designing
  an individual agent strategy that maximizes profit, a decentralized trading
  mechanism that determines market prices based on the sum of excess energy
  bids from all agents, and a global energy stability control that employs
  the collective V2G energy consumption to follow a predetermined curve.
  Simulation results using real-world data demonstrate the effectiveness
  of the proposed V2G system.  The code for this project is available at
  \url{https://github.com/Chenyuekang/V2G}.  Although this work has
  already been utilized in a pilot project, it is open to further
  development and testing.  Note that real-world implementation may
  require additional safety protocols to prevent V2G devices from
  consuming energy from the grid when they are unable to supply energy
  back to the grid, and to handle situations where vehicles are
  unable to connect to the grid when they are parked.  This can be

This foliation is then used to demonstrate the existence of a contact form in a neighborhood of the cone, with a specific structure defined by a contact coefficient that meets certain conditions. This, in turn, enables the construction of a Legendrian submanifold with a specified convex smooth boundary within the cone's interior. Ultimately, this analysis underpins the proof of a significant result in Legendrian therapy, wherein a distinguished class of Legendrian submanifolds is shown to be embeddable within a specified domain that includes a convex Euclidean space. The proof employs a novel, progressively iterative approach to constructing a Legendrian submanifold that is topologically equivalent to a given one, with a smooth embedding in a series of convex polyhedra. The process begins with an inner shell of the given submanifold and successively refines it, expanding the process to a global domain if necessary. The strategy relies on the application of a useful tool called the "suspension bundle," which is an important component in the proof, along with the insights gained from the analysis of a specific type of Legendrian submanifold called a "standard horn." The standard horn serves as a fundamental building block in the construction of a Legendrian therapy, with a structure that can be thought of as a combination of a set of radii and a collection of disks, each located on the surface of a sphere of a specific radius. The construction of the standard horn from a given set of radii is achieved through an extension of the previously mentioned process of Legendrian therapy, along with the addition of a feature called "tines." The tines are formed by a process that can be viewed as an iterative, layered unfolding of the sphere, with each layer comprising a stack of disks, each located on the surface of a sphere of a specific radius. The construction of the standard horn is significant because it enables the recovery of the original Legendrian submanifold from its therapy. The recovery process involves an expansion of the therapy along the tines, with a resulting structure that can be described as a collection of horns, with a global, open-ended version that can be thought of as a collection of horns extending to infinity. The recovery process also highlights the importance of a feature called "neck" regions, which serve as transitional areas that connect the parts of the therapy.

As a result, there is a pressing need to develop linear algebra algorithms that can function on these flawed machines. Finally, we outline the steps to execute a divide-conquer algorithm on a realistic Quantum computer, and provide a theoretical framework for evaluating the error of a divide-conquer algorithm. Despite significant progress in quantum mechanics, all existing methods rely on approximating molecular wavefunctions and calculating related properties from them.  This study investigates the performance of various methods in predicting NMR shieldings, specifically by comparing mean absolute errors with experimental data.  Analyzing a broad set of small to complex molecules, we find that density functional theory with meta-GGA functionals yields the best results, followed in order by post-DFT, coupled-cluster, and Hartree-Fock methods.  Furthermore, optimizing parameters for specific types of molecules shows that tighter parameterization leads to better performance, although even the best schemes struggle with certain molecular features, such as bond lengths over 1.5 angstroms and functional groups containing heavy elements.  To address these limitations, we propose combining quantum mechanics with continuum models of solvation and incorporating vibrational corrections, suggesting potential avenues for improving response property simulations.  Ultimately, this research aims to guide users in selecting methods for specific molecular types and to pave the way for more accurate simulations in chemistry and biology.  An accompanying code provides an easy-to-use framework for evaluating the performance of response property methods in NMR and related simulations.  This framework can be applied to a wide range of methods listed in the study, including popular codes like Gaussian, PSI4, and PySCF.  In addition to evaluating response properties, the code also calculates mean absolute errors with experimental data, providing a quantitative measure of performance that can be used to weight the importance of various factors in parameterization, such as core Hamiltonian parameters or basis sets.  By focusing on response properties rather than ground state properties, the code offers a more nuanced understanding of the performance of different methods and parameterization schemes, allowing for data analysis and guided user selection of methods for specific types of molecules.  This research and code provide a starting point for developing tighter parameterization schemes and more accurate methods for predicting response properties of molecules.  An accompanying README file and code can be found at https://github.com/respprop.  With this code, users can easily reproduce the results presented in the study, as well as explore and test new methods and parameterization schemes.  Furthermore, the code is designed to be easily extensible and adaptable to a broad range of applications in chemistry and biology. To address this challenge, we propose a novel framework called HeterGraphWave (HGWave) that converts any common first-order GNN into a non-parametric Bayesian classifier, thereby providing theoretical performance guarantees. Specifically, HGWave is derived from three fundamental assumptions about GNNs being (1) Markovian, (2) stationary, and (3) ergodic. When these assumptions are met, we show that the posterior node classification distribution given a specific node's neighborhood is an approximation of the posterior distribution that can be obtained through a Bayesian classifier whose feature is the node's neighborhood. We then leverage this insight to prove that the error rate of a GNN is an order of magnitude greater than the error rate of this hypothetical Bayesian classifier, whose feature is any arbitrary graph signal. We validate our framework through numerical experiments and apply it to provide an intuitive explanation of node classification in GNNs as an approximate Bayesian classifier of graph signals that includes nodes of interest and their neighbors. We also explore the possibility of training GNNs as Bayesian classifiers, though we find that existing optimization problems that train GNNs as classifiers under specific constraints do not yield Bayesian classifiers, highlighting the significance of this framework as a theoretical tool rather than a practical method for training GNNs. We believe that the HGWave framework offers a novel theoretical perspective on the underlying mechanics of GNNs that can be utilized in various settings, such as designing robust training procedures, analyzing the impact of graph sampling methods, and incorporating prior knowledge regarding graph structures.   To address this issue, we've developed a decentralized learning approach called Asynchronous Partially Observed Federated Learning (APOFL), combining both features and time efficiency.

  In APOFL, agents learn independent models based on their local observations, while the framework ensures that their policies optimize a decentralized collective reward.

As a result, there is growing interest in photometa technology across various fields. However, as this field continues to evolve, it's essential to develop more comprehensive photometa-related database systems that can process increasingly complex queries. Currently, research focuses mainly on optimizing low-level photometa hardware, while the higher-level database management layer is being largely overlooked. To address this limitation, we present MetaDB, a column-store database system specifically designed to manage and process data across a large-scale photometa network. To address storage and query processing challenges, MetaDB employs a hybrid storage architecture that combines a column-store index with a mark-and-sweep garbage collector, enabling it to efficiently handle memory leaks in photometa devices. Furthermore, MetaDB incorporates a global coordinator node that oversees a decentralized database architecture, allowing it to process complex join queries across the network while minimizing communication costs. We have implemented MetaDB as a proof-of-concept using Pure64 and OpenPhotometra, and our experimental results show that it can process large-scale queries at a fraction of the time required by existing solutions. Ultimately, MetaDB serves as a foundational design for future photometa database systems. This research extends previous work by allowing the driving time series to be long-memory processes, specifically including Gaussian memory processes and certain types of fractional Brownian motions as examples. In particular, it is shown that the convergence in expectation of the Euler scheme holds when the driving time series has a Hurst exponent greater than 1/3, which cannot be replaced by a lower threshold without additional assumptions. This research also compares the results to the existing literature based on moment convergence and tail convergence, revealing that the condition of a Hurst exponent greater than 1/3 is necessary in many cases. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that under certain conditions, the convergence in expectation of the Euler scheme is equivalent to the convergence of the driving time series's mixing rate, which may be of independent interest. Based on a newly established inequality, this equivalent condition can be met when the driving time series satisfies certain statistical properties, such as having a second-order strong mixing condition or a finite third moment. Based on these findings, it is recommended that researchers prioritize using the strong mixing condition over other conditions when studying the convergence of the Euler scheme, as it is more informative and easier to verify in practice. Based on a previously established result and the newly established inequality, it is possible to derive an estimable parameter for the convergence in expectation of the Euler scheme, which is shown to be sharp when the driving time series is a fractional Brownian motion. This research also addresses the issue of the Euler scheme's convergence in probability, as well as the convergence of a discrete-time approximation scheme driven by random steps, for stochastic differential equations driven by rough paths. This research is accompanied by numerical examples and a supplementary material that includes the proof of a result on the convergence in expectation of the Euler scheme with a random time step size, as well as a result on the convergence in probability of the Euler scheme with a random time step size, which may be of independent interest. A new class of models is introduced that generalizes both multi-stage decision processes and partially observed stochastic processes. We demonstrate that any problem that can be optimized under a partially observed stochastic process can be reformulated as a multi-stage decision process with complete information, albeit at the cost of increased model complexity. Furthermore, we establish that partially observed stochastic processes are equivalent to two-stage processes with recursive decomposition, exposing the intricacies of discrete-time partially observed linear systems. Moreover, we provide a new analysis of the existing results in [8], correcting and expanding on their findings. Finally, we outline a possible approach to solving a specific instance of the problem that arises from controlling a partially observed stochastic process. The paper's conclusions summarize the key insights gained, while an appendix provides supplementary proofs and calculations.  The paper's main contribution compares and contrasts the problem of optimizing partially observed stochastic processes with the related problem of controlling a stochastic process with complete information, highlighting the additional challenges posed by partial observability, and presents a case study involving a linear system with both external influences and internal dynamics. The research presented in this paper has been previously published in [8], although with some key differences, and is related to the problems of risk-sensitive reinforcement learning and policy gradient reinforcement learning. This approach involves designing a controller that ensures system safety in the presence of unknown parameters, external disturbances, or component failures. Unlike traditional methods that prioritize performance and efficiency, fault-tolerant control prioritizes safety above all else.

  This work presents a novel control strategy that incorporates safety constraints and guarantees system stability even if some components fail. We utilize a robust model predictive control framework that takes into account unknown parameters, external disturbances, and component failures. Unlike existing methods that focus on minimizing performance costs, our approach prioritizes safety above all else.

  We apply this control strategy to a series of examples, including a pendulum system, a robotic arm, and a thermocouple system. Our results show that our approach ensures system stability and safety in the presence of component failures, external disturbances, and unknown parameters. 

  We further establish that our control strategy meets safety and performance guarantees, even if some components fail. This is achieved by creating a robust MPC scheme that considers all possible system behaviors, including those resulting from component failures. 

  We conclude that designing a controller that prioritizes safety above performance can lead to unexpected results - ensuring the system remains stable and efficient, even in the presence of component failures, external disturbances, and unknown parameters. 

  We hope this work inspires further research in fault-tolerant control and encourages developers to prioritize safety in their control designs. 

  We also provide open-source code for designing and implementing our fault-tolerant control strategy. 

  We believe that making our code publicly available will accelerate progress in the field and facilitate the development of safe, efficient, and reliable systems. 

  We finally present a case study involving an industrial robot arm and demonstrate how our control strategy can be applied to real-world systems. 

  We also outline potential future directions for our work, including extending our control strategy to accommodate more complex systems, exploring alternative optimization objectives, and investigating the practical implications of prioritizing safety above performance.

This study employs numerical simulations to investigate the edge behavior of a Wilson-Dirac Hamiltonian for a two-dimensional $s\!=\!1$ Heisenberg antiferromagnet on a square lattice, assuming its approximate equivalence to the three-dimensional Heisenberg antiferromagnet. Specifically, previous work assumed that the Jacobi operator can be expressed as a divergence for a (2+1)-dimensional spacetime, albeit without providing a clear justification for this assumption.  In this study, we show that this assumption is invalid and leads to an inaccuracy in the divergence of the energy flux for the Alcubierre warp drive solution.  As an alternative, we employ an explicit computation of the Jacobi operator and show that it cannot be represented as a divergence in the spacetime at hand. In addition, we find that this issue is also relevant to other spacetime geometries that involve a similar expansion of the Jacobi operator.  As an example, we compute both the expansion and Jacobi operator for an apparent horizon in a (2+1)-dimensional spacetime.  In this context, we observe that the choice of a particular horizon slice is not merely a matter of geometric interpretation, as it is also linked to an energy flux that is both physically meaningful and locally conserved.  As such, we propose that a more precise formulation of the energy flux that is associated with the warp drive geometry should be based on a divergence that is represented by a sum of both a bulk term and a surface term, as this approach provides a clearer insight into the physical significance of the associated boundary terms.   Research in both cognition and musicology has identified several key
  processes involved in this recognition, including the automatic grouping
  of sound patterns, the distinction between expected and unexpected
  musical events, and the recall of remembered patterns. To better understand
  these processes, this study analyzed the recognition of abstract themes
  and solo instrumental melodies using functional magnetic resonance
  equipment. Subjects were asked to identify repeated melodies, both
  expected and unexpected, and to remember the opening sections of new
  melodies. The results showed that the repeated areas of the brains
  activated by the automatic grouping of sound patterns, the expectation
  of musical events, and the recall of remembered patterns are similar, and
  are located in the left and right superior and middle temporal
  lobes, respectively. The analysis of this data also revealed that the
  distinction between expected and unexpected musical events is processed
  in the right hemisphere, and that the right temporal lobe is more
  active when remembering the opening sections of new melodies rather than
  abstract themes. This study provides new insights into the neural
  processes involved in the recognition and memory of musical themes, and
  suggests that the composition of music evokes a unique set of neural
  processes that are similar to, yet distinct from, the processes
  associated with the recognition and memory of non-musical abstract
  concepts. This research also highlights the potential benefits of
  incorporating music cognition into the study of cognitive neuroscience,
  and the potential advantages of using music in the study of neural
  plasticity, memory, and the effects of aging on the brain. This study
  demonstrates that music can be utilized in an innovative manner to
  elicit a wide range of neural processes in various brain regions, and
  suggests that music may serve as a versatile tool in a broad spectrum
  of cognitive neuroscience applications. This research further proposes
  several potential music cognition research projects, including the
  investigation of the neural processes involved in the creation of
  music, the analysis of the unique neural processes associated with
  music, and the utilization of music in an innovative manner to
  elicit specific neural processes in various brain regions. This study
  also outlines a proposed music cognition research project that aims
  to investigate the neural processes involved in the recognition and
  memory of abstract concepts and musical themes through the analysis
  of brain wave patterns before and after the presentation of music.

a single infected individual, over the course of their infectious period, is referred to as the basic reproduction number (R0).  This value is crucial in assessing the severity of an epidemic's initial stage.  However, determining R0 at the outset of an epidemic is often challenging, as it is typically calculated using data from the epidemic's later stages.  This study aims to utilize contact patterns from the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic in Sweden to estimate the time-dependent R0 values during the country's initial stages of the epidemic.  A key factor in achieving this goal is the use of non-linear filtering techniques to accurately model changing R0 values while also accounting for variations in reported cases.  Based on the analyzed data, we observe that R0 initially exceeded 1 in Stockholm, leading to unchecked epidemic growth, whereas in rural areas of Sweden, the R0 value remained consistently above 1 for a longer period.  Furthermore, we found that non-pharmaceutical interventions implemented in Sweden did result in a decrease in R0 values, albeit to a limited extent.  The proposed model also allows for the assessment of future epidemic development based on various scenarios, which we tested by adjusting the R0 values.  To validate the model's effectiveness, we used synthetic data generated from the same model used in the study, and the results showed that the model accurately predicted the number of new cases over the course of the epidemic. This challenge arises when you want to apply the look-alike technique to a specific person in a video, but the process fails due to movement, rotation, or other variations in the target's appearance. To resolve this issue, we propose an innovative approach, the Variational Gaussian Mixture Model (VGMM), which combines the strengths of Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs) and Variational Inference (VI).   known as multichip distance estimation, which can be performed with a 
  minimalistic protocol to ensure security and privacy. Researchers have previously 
  proposed several protocols for multichip distance estimation, yet the issue 
  of securing these estimations against malicious behavior remains unresolved. In 
  this paper, we tackle the problem of creating an immutable and verifiable 
  log of device-proximities, which can be achieved under the assumption that 
  devices can engage in a small number of secure multichip distance measurements. 
  We present a proximity estimation protocol called ProVeriD, which incorporates 
  verifiable multichip distance estimations and incorporates a decentralized 
  reputation system to penalize devices that provide erroneous proximity 
  estimations. Furthermore, ProVeriD enables devices to create a shared, 
  tamper-proof document detailing their proximities and allows them to 
  challenge any document that omits a falsified entry. In the process, we 
  introduce a novel hash-based tree construction mechanism known as 
  VeriDTree. This mechanism supports the addition, removal, and verification 
  of nodes within the tree structure, effectively making it an efficient 
  solution for managing large collections of verifiable, timestamped data 
  (files). In the absence of a trusted third party, ProVeriD employs a 
  decentralized reputation system that utilizes a binary tree of hashes to 
  validate the integrity of the document branches and determines the 
  responsibility of a particular node by employing a recursive hash-based 
  proof. This approach can be applied to various scenarios, including 
  the secure insertion and removal of documents, as well as the 
  verification of a document against a specific set of rules. 
  Additionally, ProVeriD incorporates a mechanism for encrypting and 
  managing access to document branches, enabling devices to securely

  environment. This approach has implications for various applications,

  interactions, and other verifiable events that require robust 
  anti-tampering protection.

  account the inherent time variability of the data and, in this specific case, 
  the evolution of future sessions. To address this, we developed a framework 
  that employs temporal factors to focus the compression on the most significant 
  sections of the data, producing a model we tested on a genuine medical

  standard approach in terms of accuracy, and as an added bonus, this method 
  can be used to forecast future sessions. This discovery led to the creation 
  of a strategy that incorporates session-specific information to further 
  refine the model, resulting in our final proposed framework. This framework 
  has multiple benefits, including enhanced performance, a predictive capacity 
  that can be utilized to guide system design, and most notably, the ability 
  to efficiently manage memory while accommodating the growth of future sessions 
  without the need for explicit session truncation.  Ultimately, our results 
  demonstrated that employing a recurrent neural network with a gateway module 
  led to the best performance compared to alternative approaches, and this

  module, which differentiates it from conventional hidden state updates.

  this approach can be ascribed to the selective overwriting of hidden states

  hypothesis, we conducted an additional experiment that removed the gateway 
  module's ability to adapt to sequence length, and the result showed that 
  longer sequences with a higher degree of diversity lead to a better 
  representation of the data, ultimately resulting in enhanced performance.

This new method also reveals an interesting connection between analytic solutions to these equations and certain well-known mathematical constructs, such as holomorphic surfaces and Lefschetz hyperstructure, which provides further evidence for the significance of these structures in fields like physics and mathematics. This new structure encompasses both the Nomura differential algebraic structure and the Ito Oono differential algebraic structure, and is characterized by a set of rules that define how analytic functions of higher dimensions behave when applied to specific types of variables. To prepare for the Ariel data, we conducted a detailed analysis of the coma and dust shell emissions of comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko, a comet that was closely observed during its 2014-2015 close approach to the Sun. Using a sophisticated model of cometary physics and ground-based measurements of dust particles, we gathered comprehensive information about comet 69P, including its gas and dust composition, particle sizes, and the orientation of dust particles. We then used this information to simulate the X-ray emissions of the comet using a computational model called the Thermal Compton Scattering Code, which takes into account the interactions between cometary particles and X-ray emissions. The results of our simulation accurately match the observed X-ray emissions of the comet and reveal that the X-ray emissions from the coma and dust shell can be distinguished based on the orientation of dust particles, specifically in the 1800-2000 degree range, where the orientation of particles allows for more efficient scattering of X-rays. Combining this information, we found that the X-ray emissions from the coma and dust shell can be explained by the scattering of the diffuse solar X-ray emission rather than the emissions from the solar wind. We also discovered that the scattered X-ray emissions can take the form of a prominent arc or a wide fan-shaped region, and that the size of the arc or fan-shaped region is determined by the distance of the comet's tail and the orientation of the dust particles. We conclude that the distribution of the scattered X-ray emissions holds significant implications for understanding the shape of the coma and the dynamics of cometary particles, and that the Ariel mission will be capable of detecting this feature, providing valuable insights into the physics of comets. When studying their decidability, researchers consider two primary aspects: the magnitude of an automaton and its underlying clock structure. This study explores the boundary of decidability in event-clock automata, particularly those without assumptions about completeness. For this variant, we show that we can distinguish between languages recognized by event-clock automata if the difference in their size is $2^k$, where $k$ represents the number of variables in the automaton. To tackle this problem, we've developed two large-scale datasets, NewsTalk and FinTalk, containing online conversation transcripts about general news and financial topics respectively. Each dataset includes corresponding summary labels for discussions centered on particular news stories or financial events. We've also created two automatic conversation summary evaluation metrics, one measuring the similarity of conversation and summary keywords, the other based on keyword matching with additional context consideration. In experiments using these datasets and evaluation methods, we've observed interesting patterns, such as the correlation between conversation and summary similarity, and the difficulty finchat summaries pose due to often present legal disclaiming language. To address the challenge of generating precise summaries from these conversations, we've compared several pre-existing models, finding that the T5 text compression paradigm is particularly effective in this specific task. To facilitate further research and summary generation from online conversation sources, we're making NewsTalk and FinTalk publicly available.  We've found that pre-trained compression models on these datasets require additional fine-tuning to produce high-quality summaries, and have included an appendix with implementation details to aid interested developers in building their own summary generation models.  We're excited about the potential for future research on this problem, and invite the research community to contribute towards more effective online conversation summary generation methods. Although these models can accurately represent relationships, determining the underlying causality from them involves significant computational expenses, hindering their potential for large-scale applications. In contrast, learning the underlying graphs of Bayesian causal models from data can be accomplished using established methods, albeit with certain assumptions, such as knowing the set of possible symptoms. In clinical settings, this information is typically available, making it feasible to employ existing algorithms to infer the underlying causality. We introduce a novel approach, the Single-Path algorithm, which takes account of treatment decisions made in sequence and provides an estimate of the underlying Bayesian causal graph that adheres to the constraints of causality, as defined by Pearl's do-operator. The proposed algorithm generates two separate sets of nodes in the estimated graph: direct causes and intermediate factors generated by the single-path causal process. We establish the validity of the proposed algorithm by showing that it respects the single-path structure and accurately infers the underlying causality, as verified through synthetic and real-world data experiments. The results indicate that the Single-Path algorithm delivers superior performance in comparison to the standard causal reinforcement learning approach. The proposed method's computational efficiency and effectiveness of the generated graphs make it a suitable choice for utilizing pre-existing knowledge about the set of possible symptoms, as demonstrated by an analysis of various feature sets commonly encountered in clinical settings. The paper also addresses the issue of intermediate nodes by establishing their significance and exploring methods to distinguish between them and direct causes, such as employing a type filter. The research culminates in a case study of a real-world dataset comprising 53 continuous features, yielding a marked reduction in the number of estimated nodes while maintaining the accuracy of the estimated graph. The paper concludes by outlining potential extensions of the Single-Path algorithm, such as incorporating temporal information and generalizing to time-dependent causality, as well as exploring alternative type filters. The code for the Single-Path algorithm is available at https://github.com/causalanalyzer/single_path. The paper further provides an introduction to Bayesian causal models, the single-path structure, and an approach to validate the estimated graphs. The appendix contains additional results, additional type filter discussions, and an analysis of the impact of varying parameters.   polarization due to scattering from a given region of a disk, also
  estimating the influence of already present magnetic fields in young stars
  on the observed polarization. The results of the study have been used to
  create models of protostellar disks with the aim of reproducing the observed

  chemical processes. The research also explored the potential for future

  signatures in these objects. The team has made their model data publicly
  available on the CIGS database. The study suggests that the influence of

However, potential hardware malfunctions or cyber attacks could compromise the integrity of these systems, posing a significant risk to classified information and sensitive data.  Side-channel attacks, which exploit hidden information from the hardware, and physical attacks, which target the actual components, can significantly impair the security and dependability of such systems.  Therefore, designing hardware that can securely and dependably accelerate low-memory ANN operations is crucial.  This article presents a memory-efficient ANN technology called Binary Neural Network (BNN) and integrates it with a Hardware Neural Network Intrinsic Security (H2NIS) framework to provide robust security features.  Specifically, BNN is applied to classify various types of embedded data, and the resulting design is optimized for a Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) and exhibits high accuracy while requiring minimal memory.  The proposed design demonstrates a high level of resilience in the face of various hardware malfunctions and cyber attacks, and provides tangible performance and security benefits.  Finally, several case studies are provided to showcase the practicality of BNN-based H2NIS in real-world applications.  The code for this project is available on GitHub at https://github.com/AbdullahAlshomrani/BNN_H2NIS.  Overall, our results show that using BNN-based H2NIS yields the best results compared to other memory-efficient ANN technologies in various classification tasks.  Specifically, it achieves the highest accuracy of 99.79% with a low memory footprint of 4.8 KB, processing real-world embedded data at a speed of 13.45 ms.  The design can be optimized further to enhance its speed, and several research opportunities are identified to enhance the design's security features.  Ultimately, BNN-based H2NIS is an ideal solution for secure and dependable ANN-based embedded systems with limited resources. SSP) is a classic challenge 
  in operations research and management science. This problem involves 
  allocating and managing production tasks on a limited number of machines, 
  where each task can be performed by any available machine, and tasks are 
  linked by requirements. The problem's goal is to maximize profit by 
  selecting a subset of available jobs and scheduling them accordingly, 
  subject to production constraints and resource limitations. 

  This paper introduces a two-stage approach to solve the dynamic job-shop 
  scheduling problem with multiple machines and varied job availability. 

  In the first stage, an approximation algorithm is applied to determine 
  candidate jobs based on their potential profit and a measure of their 
  feasibility. This stage employs a limited look-ahead approach to assess 
  the feasibility of job bundles. 

  In the second stage, a constrained version of the Knapsack problem is 
  solved to select the most profitable subset of scheduled jobs. 

  The paper provides theoretical performance guarantees for the two-stage 
  solution and demonstrates its practical value through computational 
  experiments. 

  Specifically, it shows that the two-stage solution guarantees at least 
  50% of the profit achievable through optimal offline solutions, subject to 
  certain constraints, and exhibits promising results in a dynamic job-shop 
  setting with multiple machines. 

  Further analysis highlights the value of look-ahead consideration in 
  this framework. 

  Finally, an open question regarding improving the approximation ratio 
  is posed. 

  The code for the experiments is available online.

To address this knowledge gap, we employed x-ray photoemission electron microscopy with variable energy and angle to spatially and spectrally resolve photoelectron distributions from graphene. This allowed us to directly obtain detailed spectra and angular distributions of photoelectrons, which we then used to extract key optical parameters of graphene. By comparing these measurements to simulations, we identified and distinguished two distinct photoelectric processes in graphene, attributed to $\pi$ and $\sigma$ orbital interactions with light.  These processes exhibit distinct spatial and angular distributions of photoelectrons and varying intensity across the graphene surface.  Our comprehensive data and simulation results confirm that the apparent single-atom photoelectric response of graphene arises from localized $\sigma$ orbital interactions, whereas the apparent long-range field of graphene results from the combination of $\pi$ orbital interactions and the scattering of photoelectrons from the graphene surface potential.  We also demonstrated that the visible free carrier plasma field of graphene can be resolved and its spatial profile correlated with the work function of graphene.  Furthermore, we found that the free carrier plasma field has a periodic modulation along the edge of the graphene lattice, offering a direct optical approach to studying the spatial distribution of electrons in graphene.  Our research provides a precise and detailed understanding of the complex photoelectric processes in graphene.  We have made our data and simulation code available online to facilitate further study of this work.  Finally, we propose potential applications of our findings, including using the spatial and angular distributions of photoelectrons to improve graphene-based photodetectors and the modulation of the edge state field as a method to enhance visible free carrier plasma fields.  Our results serve as a starting point for designing future experiments and devices based on graphene and similar 2D materials. for long-distance operations. To address this limitation, researchers have 
been working on extending the range of UAS through Multi-UAV communication,

systems. The proposed optimization model considers the range extension

suggested that future air traffic management systems integrate communication 
aspects into their protocols to fully capitalize on the range extension 
capability of UAS. The proposed optimization model has been validated 
through simulations based on real-world scenarios.

We establish that these systems are mutually singular with respect to measures, allowing us to establish the unique representation of measures that are invariant under their natural action. flexible framework in Release 14 for Radio Access Network Function

rigid, adaptable base station configurations, using Pseudo-Physical Entities 
(PPEs). Each PPE represents a base station component, running on a virtual
